subtopic: 2.7 Hypothesis Testing ｜假設檢定
subtopic_raw: 1.7 Hypothesis Testing ｜假設檢定
stem: The purpose of a test is to decide whether a sample result is consistent with a stated population value. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.A: Accepting H0 proves that the hypothesized value is true with probability 1-α.
choices.B: A large p-value proves Ha, because Ha is “no relationship.”
choices.C: H0 is the claim one tries to reject. You never prove Ha in a logical sense; rejecting H0 is what licenses concluding Ha.

choices.C: not a legitimate pair, because H0 must always be µ=0.

choices.A: failing to reject a false H0. That probability is α.

stem: Households become keen to spend (a demand shock). Separately, an oil-cost spike hits (a supply shock). Which policy reading is most accurate?

choices.A: Ease after the demand shock and tighten after the oil shock, so that real rates stay constant.
choices.B: Tighten after the demand shock. A negative supply shock can raise inflation while reducing output — a policy trade-off that depends on inflation persistence, expectations, output, and objectives. Tightening after an oil-cost spike is not the same mechanical response: it would add demand weakness on top of already higher costs.
choices.C: Tighten after both shocks, because any rise in inflation is a case for higher policy rates.

choices.A: The 40, 35, and 25 units each meet the 10% revenue test. Together they are 100/108 ≈92.6% of company revenue, so the 75% aggregate external-revenue coverage test is already met. The 8 unit is below 10% of revenue, assets, and profit, so it need not be disclosed as a reportable segment.

stem: Two bids are at the same price in a typical order-driven book. A hidden bid arrives first. A displayed bid at that same price arrives later. Which ranking is most accurate?

choices.A: Price priority first. At the same price, displayed liquidity generally ranks ahead of hidden liquidity, so the later displayed bid is ahead of the earlier hidden bid. Time priority then applies inside the displayed class or the hidden class.
choices.B: The hidden bid executes first because it arrived first: at a given price, time priority automatically outranks display status.
choices.C: Hidden size is treated as more aggressive than displayed size at the same price, so the hidden bid is ahead of the later displayed bid.

stem: Under Ricardian equivalence, taxpayers treat new government debt as future taxes, so the sovereign is indifferent between taxing now and issuing any maturity. A debt manager still cares about:

choices.A: only the fallen-angel downgrade path of the Treasury, because Ricardian equivalence removes rollover risk.
choices.B: rollover risk and interest-rate risk, which is why issuance is spread across the curve.
choices.C: replacing the trustee with a repo counterparty so that duration gap is always zero.

choices.A: identical in credit risk to the toll-road bond, because municipal bonds never default.
choices.B: a revenue bond, because any municipal issue is repaid only from one project.
choices.C: a general obligation bond and typically lower credit risk than the project-only revenue bond.

subtopic_raw: Sequential-Pay CMBS and Time Tranching ｜CMBS 順序分層與時間分層
stem: In a sequential-pay CMBS, which pairing is correct?

choices.A: Senior and junior share losses and prepayments pro rata in every sequential-pay deal, by definition of sequential.
choices.B: Junior / subordinate tranches generally absorb credit losses first; principal collections and pre-payments generally pay the designated earlier / senior sequential class first.
choices.C: Junior tranches receive prepayments first and absorb credit losses last, because “junior” means first cash.

choices.A: both payoffs equal zero, because any contract struck at F0(T) expires worthless when ST is below F0.
choices.B: the forward’s value is negative (ST - F0); the call’s payoff is max(0, ST - F0) = 0.

stem: After initiation, a forward differs from a futures most accurately in that:

choices.A: the contracted price is reset every day to the spot, so a forward’s remaining value is always zero, like a futures.
choices.B: both sides post variation margin daily, so a forward has no credit risk after the first mark.

stem: A copper fabricator already holds copper inventory and wants to hedge the price risk of that inventory. Copper futures are positively correlated with the inventory. The hedge is:

choices.A: short copper futures: a fall in copper reduces inventory value, and the short futures gains in that same state.
choices.B: long copper calls only, because a futures hedge is impossible once inventory is on the balance sheet.

stem: A wire plant has no copper inventory and must buy copper in two months for a fixed-price customer order. Copper futures are positively correlated with the cash copper the plant will need. The hedge is:

choices.A: short the customer order, because a commercial hedge is always a sale of the finished good in the futures market.
choices.B: long copper futures: the existing exposure is a planned purchase (short the commodity), so the futures position that offsets a rise in copper is a long.
choices.C: short copper futures, because every industrial user of copper should sell futures.

stem: A wheat grower will harvest and sell wheat at the harvest-date cash price and wants to lock in a selling price. Wheat futures move with cash wheat. The hedge is:

choices.A: short wheat futures: the grower is already long the crop, so a price decline that hurts the harvest is offset by a short-futures gain.
choices.B: long wheat futures, because growing wheat is a use of land and users always buy futures.
choices.C: long wheat puts and long wheat futures together, because a hedge must always add a put to a long futures.

stem: Which statement about early exercise of puts is most accurate?

choices.A: Cash distributions do not create an early-exercise argument for puts — a lower asset price helps the put. A deep-ITM put can still be exercised early for cash timing: if the underlying has fallen to zero, exercising collects X now; a European put collects only the present value of X at expiration. American puts can therefore be priced above otherwise identical European puts.
choices.B: American and European puts always have the same value, because a put is never exercised early.
choices.C: Dividends create the same early-exercise argument for puts as for calls, so every dividend makes the American put richer.

choices.A: is available only for net-investment hedges, never for cash-flow or fair-value hedges.

choices.C: lets the derivative offset the hedged transaction or balance-sheet item and reduces reported volatility.

choices.A: by setting every derivative’s value equal to its intrinsic value S - X or X - S.

choices.A: sell the quoted forward, buy the asset with funds borrowed at r, deliver at T, repay the loan, and keep the gap.

stem: After initiation of a plain vanilla interest-rate swap, which statement is most accurate?

choices.A: The swap’s value stays zero for life, because the price is constant and price equals value.
choices.B: The fixed rate is reset each period to the new par swap rate, so the contract cannot have MTM.
choices.C: The swap’s price — the fixed rate in the contract — stays constant. The swap’s value starts at zero and then moves as market rates move.

stem: A treasurer pays 3.60% fixed and receives MRR on a 10,000,000 notional vanilla swap, period 0.5 year. Current MRR is 4.20%. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.A: The treasurer has an MTM loss, because paying fixed is the same risk as owning a fixed-rate bond.
choices.B: Because current MRR exceeds 3.60%, the remaining swap as a whole must have a positive total MTM; the 30,000 receipt is that total MTM.
choices.C: The treasurer receives 30,000 for the current settlement period. That current-period receipt alone is not sufficient to determine the total MTM value of the remaining swap without information about the remaining term structure / forward rates.

choices.A: a loss: the client pays the higher floating rate and still receives the old fixed rate. An increase in expected future short-term rates lowers the value of this side — the same direction as a long fixed-rate bond when yields rise.
choices.B: zero, because the swap price does not change after initiation.
choices.C: a gain, because “receive fixed” sounds like the client’s coupon has been reset higher.

choices.A: each worth zero on its own, because every forward commitment is reset daily like a futures.
choices.B: each worth the swap’s current MTM, so n periods imply n times the swap value.
choices.C: off-market (not each worth zero on its own). Because the swap is worth zero at initiation, the off-market FRA values sum to zero.

stem: A private equity fund has committed capital of 200, of which 60 has been called. A 2% PE management fee in the sources is most likely charged on:

choices.A: 60, the same AUM base a hedge-fund management fee uses.
choices.B: 140, the uncalled commitment only.
choices.C: 200, which is why early reported returns can be negative before much capital is at work.

choices.B: any combination of T-bills and a well-diversified fund; its slope is that fund’s Sharpe ratio.

stem: An asset has β = 0 and a stand-alone standard deviation of 22%. The most accurate statement is:

choices.A: the asset is risk-free, because β = 0 is the definition of a risk-free asset.
choices.B: the asset has no measured systematic sensitivity; it need not be risk-free, because idiosyncratic volatility can still be large.
choices.C: the asset’s total risk is zero, because only beta is priced.

stem: A concentrated three-stock book has E(R) = 13%, Rf = 3%, σ = 20%, and β = 1.25. For ranking this book against other undiversified books, the more appropriate ratio is:

choices.A: Sharpe = 0.50, because unsystematic risk still matters and the denominator should be total risk.
choices.B: Treynor = 0.08, because only beta is ever the correct denominator.
choices.C: Jensen’s alpha, because any book with a beta can be ranked on SML residual alone.

stem: A client has a short horizon, little wealth relative to liabilities, and a strong desire for aggressive equity. The IPS risk objective should most likely reflect:

choices.A: ability to bear risk, which is low; willingness does not override a thin financial capacity.
choices.B: the average of ability and willingness, because objectives must be jointly feasible by blending.
choices.C: willingness, because the IPS exists to implement the client’s stated preferences.

stem: Rf = 2%, E(Rm) = 10%, β = 1.25. An analyst’s forecast return is 14%. Using CAPM, the stock is:

choices.A: undervalued; required return is 12% and the forecast sits above the SML.
choices.B: overvalued; required return is 12% and 14% is therefore too high a price.
choices.C: fairly priced, because any forecast that uses a beta of 1.25 must lie on the SML.
